working_title: The Long Night of the Neuron: How Machines Learned to Learn (1943-2026)
audience: Curious general viewers (teenagers through adults) with no assumed math or CS background, plus technically literate viewers who want real mechanics; the film must be accurate enough for practitioners and clear enough for newcomers.
central_questions: How were neural networks studied, by whom, and in which institutions, from 1943 to 2026?
In each era, what did the field believe about how to build intelligence, who dissented, and how long did that belief hold before it broke?
Which experiments actually changed minds (Perceptron Mark I, XOR, NETtalk, LeNet, ImageNet 2012, the 2017 transformer, scaling-law studies, ChatGPT), and what exactly did they show?
Why did neural networks fall out of favour twice (the AI winters), and what did classical machine learning do better in the meantime?
How does AlexNet work, and why did it end the argument about deep learning for vision?
How does the transformer work (attention, Q/K/V, multi-head, positional encoding, residual stream), and why did it take over language and then everything else?
How did ChatGPT, the founding of Anthropic and the other frontier labs, and the US-China competition over chips, talent and open-weight models reshape the field?
What is the 'current understanding' as of 2026-10-05: what is believed, what is contested, and who are today's dissenters?

topics.title: The Logical Neuron: McCulloch-Pitts, Hebb, Cybernetics and Dartmouth
questions: What exactly did McCulloch and Pitts (1943) claim a network of idealized neurons could compute, and how was it received?
What was Hebb's 1949 learning postulate in his own words?
What did the cybernetics movement (Wiener, the Macy conferences) believe about brains and machines, and who in it disagreed?
What did Turing (1950) propose about learning machines ('child machine')?
Who organized the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, what did the proposal predict, and was the neural approach represented (e.g., Minsky's SNARC, 1951)?
What was the belief of the age about how quickly machine intelligence would arrive, and how long did that optimism last?
must_cover: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' (1943)
Donald Hebb, The Organization of Behavior (1949)
Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics (1948); Macy conferences
Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950)
Marvin Minsky's SNARC (1951)
Dartmouth Summer Research Project proposal (McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, Shannon, 1955) and the 1956 workshop; the coining of 'artificial intelligence'
Logic Theorist (Newell, Simon, Shaw) as the symbolic alternative already in play
Verbatim quotes only from the original papers/proposal

topics.title: Rosenblatt's Perceptron and the First Neural Boom
questions: What was the perceptron learning rule and what did the Mark I Perceptron hardware look like (photocells, potentiometers, motors)?
What did Rosenblatt and the press claim (the 1958 Navy/New York Times coverage), and what did Rosenblatt actually write in Principles of Neurodynamics (1962)?
What was the perceptron convergence theorem and what did it guarantee?
What parallel work existed (Widrow-Hoff ADALINE/LMS, Selfridge's Pandemonium, Bernard Widrow's MADALINE)?
Who was skeptical at the time, and how were funding and attention split between perceptrons and symbolic AI?
must_cover: Frank Rosenblatt; Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory; Office of Naval Research funding
Rosenblatt 1958 Psychological Review paper; Mark I Perceptron (1958-1960); Principles of Neurodynamics (1962)
July 1958 New York Times / Navy press coverage - exact wording from archival source
Perceptron convergence theorem (Block, Novikoff 1962)
Bernard Widrow and Ted Hoff, ADALINE and the LMS rule (1960)
Oliver Selfridge, Pandemonium (1959)
Rivalry with symbolic AI (Minsky, McCarthy, Newell & Simon); Minsky and Rosenblatt as Bronx Science contemporaries (verify)
Simple mechanics of a perceptron: weighted sum, threshold, error-driven update (needed for animation)

topics.title: Perceptrons (1969), the Lighthill Report and the First AI Winter
questions: What did Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons (1969) actually prove (XOR/parity, connectedness, order limits), and what did it NOT prove about multi-layer networks?

How much did the book actually cause the decline of neural-net funding vs. other factors? (contested - source both sides, including Papert's and Minsky's later comments and the 1988 expanded edition prologue)
What happened to Rosenblatt (death in 1971) and to his program?
What did the ALPAC report (1966), Lighthill report (1973) and DARPA/Mansfield-amendment cuts say and do?
Who kept working on neural ideas during the winter (Grossberg, Fukushima's Neocognitron 1980, Amari, Kohonen, Werbos 1974 thesis, Ivakhnenko's GMDH, Linnainmaa 1970 reverse-mode differentiation)?
What was the belief of the age ('single-layer nets are a dead end; intelligence is symbol manipulation'), who dissented, and how long did it hold?
must_cover: Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert, Perceptrons (1969) and the 1988 expanded edition
XOR / parity limitation, explained mechanically
Frank Rosenblatt's death (July 1971)
ALPAC report (1966)
Sir James Lighthill, 'Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey' (1973) and the televised 1973 Royal Institution debate (Lighthill vs. Michie, McCarthy, Gregory)
Mansfield Amendment (1969/1973) and DARPA funding shifts
Winter-era dissenters: Stephen Grossberg, Kunihiko Fukushima (Neocognitron, 1980), Shun-ichi Amari, Teuvo Kohonen, Paul Werbos (1974 thesis), Alexey Ivakhnenko, Seppo Linnainmaa
Historiography debate: Olazaran's 'A Sociological Study of the Official History of the Perceptrons Controversy' (1996)

topics.title: The Connectionist Revival: Hopfield, Boltzmann Machines and Backpropagation
questions: What did Hopfield's 1982 network show and why did a physicist's paper re-legitimize neural nets?
What were Boltzmann machines (Hinton, Sejnowski, Ackley 1985) and what did they learn?
What did Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (Nature, 1986) demonstrate, and how did backpropagation work mechanically (chain rule, credit assignment, hidden representations)?
Who invented backprop? Lay out the priority dispute (Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974/1982, Parker 1985, LeCun 1985, Rumelhart et al. 1986; Schmidhuber's claims) with sources for each side.
What did the PDP volumes (1986) argue, and what was the Fodor & Pylyshyn (1988) and Pinker & Prince (1988) critique? How long did the systematicity debate last?
What landmark experiments drew public attention (NETtalk, Sejnowski & Rosenberg 1987; ALVINN, Pomerleau 1989)?
must_cover: John Hopfield, 1982 PNAS paper
Geoffrey Hinton, Terry Sejnowski, David Ackley - Boltzmann machines (1985)
David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, Ronald Williams, 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' (Nature, 1986)
Parallel Distributed Processing volumes (Rumelhart, McClelland and the PDP Research Group, 1986)
Backprop priority dispute: Linnainmaa, Werbos, Parker, LeCun, Schmidhuber's critique
Fodor & Pylyshyn (1988) 'Connectionism and cognitive architecture'; Pinker & Prince (1988) on past-tense learning
NETtalk (1987); ALVINN (1989)
Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko 1989; Hornik, Stinchcombe, White 1989)
Hinton's move to Carnegie Mellon then Toronto; CIFAR beginnings (verify dates)
Backprop mechanics clear enough to animate

topics.title: The Expert Systems Boom and the Second AI Winter
questions: What were expert systems (MYCIN, XCON/R1) and what did businesses and governments believe they would deliver?
What were Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project, the US Strategic Computing Initiative, the UK Alvey programme and MCC, and how did each end?
Why did the Lisp-machine market collapse around 1987, and how did 'AI winter' become a term (the 1984 AAAI panel warning by Schank and Minsky)?
Where did neural nets sit during the second winter - did the backprop revival also cool, and why (data, compute, vanishing gradients)?
What was the belief of the age (knowledge engineering, hand-coded rules; Cyc's bet), who dissented (Brooks's behavior-based robotics, Dreyfus's philosophical critique), and how long did it hold?
must_cover: Edward Feigenbaum and knowledge engineering; MYCIN; XCON/R1 at DEC
Japan's Fifth Generation project (1982-1992)
DARPA Strategic Computing Initiative; Alvey programme; MCC
Doug Lenat's Cyc (1984-)
Lisp machine collapse (Symbolics, LMI) ~1987
1984 AAAI 'dark ages' panel / origin of the term 'AI winter'
Hubert Dreyfus, What Computers Can't Do (1972) and What Computers Still Can't Do (1992)
Rodney Brooks, 'Elephants Don't Play Chess' (1990) and 'Intelligence without representation' (1991)

topics.title: Classical Machine Learning Ascendant: Statistics, SVMs and the Quiet Holdouts
questions: What were the dominant methods (SVMs and kernel methods, boosting, random forests, graphical models/Bayesian networks, HMMs, statistical NLP) and why did researchers prefer them (convexity, theory, guarantees, smaller data)?
What was the belief of the age about neural nets ('hard to train, no theory, local minima, black boxes'), and how long did it hold - roughly mid-1990s to ~2010?

What did neural-net holdouts achieve anyway: LeNet and MNIST (LeCun et al. 1989/1998), check-reading deployment, LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997), Hochreiter's 1991 vanishing-gradient analysis, Bengio et al. neural language model (2003)?
What was the CIFAR Neural Computation and Adaptive Perception program (2004) and the so-called 'deep learning conspiracy' of Hinton, LeCun and Bengio? Source the phrase.
What did Deep Blue (1997) and the statistical turn in speech and translation (IBM, Jelinek) show about the field's priorities? Verify the Jelinek 'fire a linguist' quote or mark it unverified.
Which paper rejections and conference attitudes (NIPS in the 2000s) do participants document?
must_cover: Vladimir Vapnik and Corinna Cortes, support-vector networks (1995); statistical learning theory
Yoav Freund and Robert Schapire, AdaBoost (1995-97); Leo Breiman, random forests (2001) and 'Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures' (2001)
Judea Pearl, Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems (1988)
Frederick Jelinek and IBM statistical speech/translation
Yann LeCun, LeNet, MNIST, 'Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition' (1998); Bell Labs
Sepp Hochreiter (1991 thesis), Hochreiter & Schmidhuber LSTM (1997)
Yoshua Bengio et al., 'A Neural Probabilistic Language Model' (2003)
IBM Deep Blue vs. Kasparov (1997)
CIFAR NCAP program (2004) and its role keeping the field alive
The Netflix Prize (2006-2009) as a showcase of classical ensembles (optional)

topics.title: The Deep Learning Renaissance: Pretraining, GPUs, ImageNet and Speech
questions: What did Hinton, Osindero & Teh (2006) and Hinton & Salakhutdinov (Science, 2006) show about layer-wise pretraining, and why did the 'deep learning' brand stick?
When and how did GPUs become the engine (Raina, Madhavan & Ng 2009; Ciresan et al. 2010-2012 at IDSIA; CUDA)?
How was ImageNet built (Fei-Fei Li, WordNet, Amazon Mechanical Turk) and what did skeptics say about it at the time? When did ILSVRC start (2010)?
How did deep nets break through in speech recognition first (Mohamed, Dahl, Hinton; Microsoft, Google, IBM; the 2012 joint IEEE Signal Processing Magazine paper)?
What did rectified linear units (Nair & Hinton 2010; Glorot et al. 2011) and dropout contribute?
What was Google Brain's 2012 'cat' experiment (Le, Ng, Dean et al.) and how was it covered?
must_cover: Hinton, Osindero & Teh, deep belief nets (2006); Hinton & Salakhutdinov (2006)
Bengio et al. greedy layer-wise training (2007); Ranzato/LeCun work
Fei-Fei Li, ImageNet (CVPR 2009), ILSVRC (2010-2017); Christiane Fellbaum / WordNet; Mechanical Turk
GPUs: Raina, Madhavan, Ng (2009); Dan Ciresan and Jurgen Schmidhuber at IDSIA
Speech: Abdel-rahman Mohamed, George Dahl, Navdeep Jaitly; Microsoft Research (Li Deng, Dong Yu); 'Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition' (2012)
ReLU; dropout (Hinton et al. 2012 arXiv)
Google Brain founding (Andrew Ng, Jeff Dean, Greg Corrado) and the 2012 unsupervised 'cat' paper
Belief of the age: 'deep nets need unsupervised pretraining' - and how quickly that belief was abandoned

topics.title: AlexNet in Depth: ImageNet 2012 and the Morning After
questions: What exactly was the AlexNet architecture (5 conv + 3 fully connected layers, filter sizes, strides, ~60M parameters, ~650K neurons), and how was it split across two GTX 580 GPUs?

What were the key ingredients and their measured effects as reported in the paper: ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, overlapping pooling, local response normalization, SGD with momentum and weight decay, training time (~5-6 days)?
What were the exact ILSVRC-2012 results (top-5 test error ~15.3% vs ~26.2% for the runner-up) and who was the runner-up?
How did Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton build it (cuda-convnet, Krizhevsky's GPU kernels), and what do participants say about how it started?
How did the computer-vision community react at the ECCV 2012 workshop in Florence? Find first-hand accounts and distinguish verified from legend.

What followed: the DNNresearch auction and Google acquisition (2013), ZFNet, VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet (2015, surpassing reported human-level top-5 error), and the claimed 'human-level' benchmark debates
What did AlexNet's first-layer filters learn (Gabor-like edges, color blobs) - useful for visualization
must_cover: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 'ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks' (NIPS 2012) - all numbers from the paper
Layer-by-layer architecture with tensor shapes (224/227 input discrepancy noted)
Two-GPU model parallelism on NVIDIA GTX 580 3GB
Data augmentation, dropout, ReLU, LRN, overlapping pooling - mechanics
ILSVRC 2012 results table (runner-up ISI team, Fisher vectors)
ECCV 2012 Florence workshop reaction (first-hand sources, e.g. Fei-Fei Li's The Worlds I See, interviews)
DNNresearch acquisition by Google (2013) and the bidding (Cade Metz, Genius Makers - verify details)
Lineage: LeNet -> AlexNet; successors ZFNet (2013), VGG (2014), GoogLeNet (2014), ResNet (He et al. 2015)
Computer History Museum release of AlexNet source code (2025, verify)
First-layer filter visualizations

topics.title: The Gold Rush: Embeddings, Sequence Models, AlphaGo and the New Labs
questions: What did word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013) show about learned meaning ('king - man + woman ~ queen'), and what are its caveats?
How did sequence-to-sequence models (Sutskever, Vinyals, Le 2014) and Bahdanau-Cho-Bengio attention (2014) change machine translation, culminating in Google Neural Machine Translation (2016)?
What were GANs (Goodfellow et al. 2014) and deep RL on Atari (DQN, Mnih et al. 2013/2015)?
Why did Google buy DeepMind (2014), and what did AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol (March 2016) show, including move 37? What did experts predict about Go before the match?
Why was OpenAI founded (December 2015), by whom, with what stated mission?
What did dissenters argue during the boom (Gary Marcus 2018 'Deep Learning: A Critical Appraisal'; adversarial examples, Szegedy et al. 2013; bias concerns, Buolamwini & Gebru 2018)?
How did the 2018 Turing Award to Bengio, Hinton and LeCun mark the official vindication?

Sutskever, Vinyals & Le seq2seq (2014); Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio attention (2014); GNMT (2016)
Ian Goodfellow, GANs (2014)
DeepMind (Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, Mustafa Suleyman); Google acquisition (2014); DQN; AlphaGo (2016); AlphaGo Zero (2017)
OpenAI founding (Dec 2015): Altman, Musk, Sutskever, Brockman and others
Facebook AI Research founded with LeCun (2013); Baidu (Andrew Ng) - early Chinese industrial AI
Adversarial examples (Szegedy et al. 2013; Goodfellow et al. 2014)
Gary Marcus's critiques; Joy Buolamwini & Timnit Gebru, Gender Shades (2018)
ACM Turing Award 2018 (announced March 2019)

topics.title: Transformers in Depth: Attention Is All You Need and the Pretraining Era
questions: Who were the eight authors of 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017), what problem were they solving at Google, and how did the name and design come about (first-hand accounts)?

Mechanically: tokens and embeddings; scaled dot-product attention softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V; why the sqrt(d_k) scaling; multi-head attention; causal masking; sinusoidal positional encodings; residual connections and layer norm; feed-forward sublayers; encoder-decoder structure. Get exact hyperparameters (d_model=512, 8 heads, 6 layers, base/big models) and the WMT 2014 BLEU results from the paper.
Why did the transformer beat RNNs/LSTMs (parallelism, path length, training cost) - per the paper's own complexity table?
How did it become the substrate for pretraining: ELMo (2018), GPT-1 (June 2018), BERT (Oct 2018), GPT-2 (Feb 2019) and the staged-release controversy, T5?

What did researchers believe about attention (is attention explanation? 'Attention is not Explanation', Jain & Wallace 2019) and what later interpretability (induction heads, Olsson et al. 2022) revealed?
What happened to the authors afterwards (all left Google; companies founded)?
must_cover: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
Exact architecture details and numbers from the paper (arXiv 1706.03762)

Comparison to RNN/LSTM and Bahdanau attention
GPT-1 (Radford et al. 2018); BERT (Devlin et al. 2018); GPT-2 and OpenAI's staged release (2019)
